ai_show_review.summary: Tight studio set with strong Candyman, but muddied mix dampens impact
ai_show_review.blurb: The five‑song studio session showcases Garcia’s soaring vocals on Candyman and Brokedown Palace, while Pigpen delivers a gritty lead on Easy Wind. Standout moments include tight jams on Easy Wind and Candyman, though the matrix broadcast suffers from muddied bass and occasional dropouts.
ai_show_review.review:
On August 30, 1970 the Grateful Dead slipped into KQED Studios for a concise five‑song set that feels more like a miniature concert than a typical studio cut. Jerry’s voice shines on “Candyman” and “Brokedown Palace,” delivering a mesmerizing vocal performance, and Pigpen’s raw, busted‑out‑of‑jail lead on “Easy Wind” adds an extra punch of energy. Phil’s bass work is solid in the room but gets buried in the quad‑broadcast mix, leaving the low end thin. The band builds tight jams around “Easy Wind” and “Candyman,” with a spirited take on “Casey Jones” that rounds out the set before closing with “Uncle John’s Band.”

The best listening source is the fair‑quality matrix recording (gd70-08-30.fm.jupile.12762.sbeok.shnf). It captures most of the performance’s power despite occasional muddiness, uneven bass, and drop‑outs that prevent it from being a clean soundboard capture. A second, very poor version exists but offers little beyond a tolerable “Candyman” segment, making the matrix tape the clear choice for fans seeking this rare studio snapshot.

best_recording.reason: Fair‑quality matrix capture retains most of the performance’s power and is far clearer than the very poor alternate version.

key_highlights: Garcia’s mesmerizing vocals on “Candyman” and “Brokedown Palace”.
Pigpen’s gritty lead vocal on “Easy Wind” described as a ‘busted‑out‑of‑jail’ performance.
